name: Uma Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the records team at the regional water company, in the old brick office next to the treatment works. There are four of us, and we keep the maps, the maintenance logs and the permits in order, so when a pipe bursts the crews know what's under the road. I've been team lead since June, after Margaret retired, and I'm still learning things she knew without thinking. Most days it's filing, checking the crews' paperwork, chasing missing signatures and answering engineers who can't find a drawing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like order, and I like knowing that when the crews go out at night, the right drawing is in the van. The hard part is the new document system head office keeps changing, which I find confusing. My fiancé Tomas is an electrician, and we're getting married at our church next August. We're saving for that, which means there's basically nothing else in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, and that a lot of people got carried away. At church and with family I'd say that real work still needs real people. I don't really go online about this kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, even a little bit of AI could hit my team, because filing and checking is what it's meant to be good at. Head office has already moved some records into the new system and cut a post when someone left. So I'd still be watching my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job properly and learn the parts of the new system I have to, but not the AI parts. I'd keep the wedding savings going, because that comes first. And I'd ask my manager, Phil, if the team's numbers are safe for next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I suppose. The job's probably fine, but money's tight with the wedding, and a cut post means more work for the three of us. It's a lot at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the AI parts. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust it with something that matters. If an AI files a pipe drawing in the wrong place, a crew could dig into a gas main. I'd rather do it by hand and know it's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you go to if something went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents, and the people at church, honestly. My dad would say work hard and keep your head down. Pastor John (the minister at our church) always says there's a job for anyone who'll turn up.

say: I'd say people got **carried away**, and real work needs real people.
I'd say it at **church and with family**, not online.
think: Even a little AI could hit **filing and checking** work like mine.
Head office already **cut a post** when someone left, so I'd watch my back.
do: Learn the parts of the **new system** I must, but not the AI parts.
Keep the **wedding savings** going as the top priority.
Ask my manager if **team numbers** are safe for next year.
feel: Uneasy about **tight money** and extra work after the cut post.
S0.quote: If an AI files a pipe drawing in the wrong place, a crew could dig into a gas main. I'd rather do it by hand and know it's right.
fieldNote: Her distrust of AI is about **safety**, not just habit.
A **cut post** has already made her wary before any AI change.
Her support network is **family and church**, not the state.

steps.text: Keep checking crew paperwork by hand and refuse AI filing
Keep paying into the wedding fund every month
Ask Phil (her manager) if the records team is safe next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company is chasing fashion and forgetting what keeps the water running. At work I'd say it to Phil and to the engineers, who'd mostly agree. I'd be polite about it, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my team is exactly the checking and planning on that card. If the system files and checks everything, they don't need four people in records, maybe one. And I'm the newest team lead and I don't use the tools, so I can see where that goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for something in the water company that's out with the crews, like a field admin or a meter reader, because that's harder to automate. I'd cut back hard, no meals out, no new clothes. And I'd talk to Tomas about a smaller wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums. It feels like the floor's been taken out from under me just as we're trying to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tomas say about a smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say fine, he never wanted the big one anyway. It's me and my mum who wanted it. Tomas (my fiancé, an electrician) would say his work is safe for years, so stop worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is he right?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, for him. People will need electricians for a long time. But I don't want to get married and then be the wife who can't bring anything in.

say: I'd say the company is **chasing fashion** over keeping water running.
I'd say it **politely** to my manager and the engineers.
think: Records work is exactly the **checking and planning** on the card.
Four people could become **one**, and I'm new and don't use the tools.
do: Look for **field work** with the crews, like meter reading.
Cut **meals out** and **new clothes** to protect the wedding money.
Talk to my fiancé about a **smaller wedding**.
feel: Like the floor's gone just as they **build a life**.
S1.quote: I don't want to get married and then be the wife who can't bring anything in.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the role** because she won't use AI tools.
Her pride shows: she wants to **contribute**, not be carried by her husband.
She'd move toward **field work** with the crews, which is hands-on.

steps.text: Apply for meter reader or field admin posts with the crews
Stop eating out and buying new clothes
Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to 50

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness to let it happen this fast, and someone should have stopped it. At church I'd say we need to look after each other. I'd also say that people will always need people, though I'm not sure I'd believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my office job is gone by 2028. Tomas's electrician work lasts until the robots, around 2031, so he'd carry us for three years. After that I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find any hands-on work with the water company, even out in the cold reading meters. We'd bring the wedding forward and make it tiny, at the church hall. And I'd lean on my parents, maybe move in with them for a bit to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and a bit ashamed, if that makes sense. I always thought hard work would be enough. Two years isn't enough time to work hard at anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider government support if it came to it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if there was nothing else. My family's always stood on its own feet. I'd go to my parents and the church before I went to the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the wedding forward rather than delay it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with all this coming, I want to be married and settled first. My grandmother married in hard times and always said that's when you need each other most. We'd do it small, but we'd do it.

say: I'd say it's **madness** to let it happen this fast.
I'd say at church that we must **look after each other**.
think: My fiancé's **electrician work** carries us until about 2031, then I don't know.
do: Find **hands-on work** with the water company, even meter reading.
Bring the wedding forward and hold it at the **church hall**.
Move in with **my parents** to save rent.
feel: Alarmed and **a bit ashamed** that hard work isn't enough.
S2.quote: I always thought hard work would be enough. Two years isn't enough time to work hard at anything new.
fieldNote: She'd turn to **family and church** before any government help.
Fast AGI makes her **bring the wedding forward**, not delay it.
Her fiancé's hands-on trade is a **three-year bridge**, and she knows it.

steps.text: Apply for any outdoor meter-reading job at the water company
Hold a small wedding at the church hall this spring
Move in with her parents to save on rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still too fast for normal families, and companies should be honest with staff. At church I'd want us to start something for people losing jobs. I'd try to be useful rather than just complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years doesn't really change where I end up. Records is thinking work, so it goes in 2031. I'd have a few years to find something else, but I'm not quick at learning new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask about moving to the water company's field side now, while there's time, and do the safety course they require. We'd have the wedding as planned, but cheaper. And I'd probably wait a year to see how fast it really comes before doing anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still, but less frantic. Five years of warning is like seeing a storm on the horizon. You know it's coming, you just don't know how bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a year. Is that wise with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, but that's me. I don't like jumping until I'm sure. Tomas says I'll wait until it's on top of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about children differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still want them, maybe sooner, honestly. I'd rather have small children while Tomas is working than wait and have nothing. My mum says babies come with their own bread.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** for normal families.
I'd want the church to start something for **people losing jobs**.
think: Records is thinking work, so it **still goes** in 2031.
I'm **not quick** at learning, so five years may not help much.
do: Ask to move to the **field side** and take the safety course.
Hold the **wedding as planned**, but cheaper.
**Wait a year** before doing anything bigger.
feel: Alarmed but less frantic, like a **storm on the horizon**.
S3.quote: Five years of warning is like seeing a storm on the horizon. You know it's coming, you just don't know how bad.
fieldNote: Five years barely changes her outcome, because she's **slow to change**.
She'd **wait a year**, even admitting it's probably unwise.
Children might come **sooner**, while her fiancé's trade is still safe.

steps.text: Ask to transfer to field work and take the safety course
Keep the August wedding but cut the budget
Wait a year to see how fast AI really arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for people to sort themselves out, if they're willing to work. At church I'd say the same thing, that God gives us time for a reason. I'd sound more confident than I'd feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'd be thirty-seven, probably with kids. Records still goes by 2036, but by then I could be on the field side or doing something else. I'd still worry about the money in between.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and do it well, and maybe move to the field side in a few years. We'd have the wedding as planned in August. And I'd ask Tomas to think about taking on an apprentice, so we've got a bit of a family business by the time the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I could breathe. Ten years feels like normal life with something worrying at the end of it. The wedding and the house matter more day to day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A family business with Tomas. What would you do in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The books, the bookings, the paperwork. Though that's the thinking work that goes first, isn't it. Maybe I'd have to learn the electrics too, which I've never thought about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever try the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Tomas's business needed it, maybe. AI tools would feel different if the business was ours and not head office forcing it on me. I'd still check everything by hand, though.

say: I'd say ten years is enough if people are **willing to work**.
I'd say at church that **God gives time** for a reason.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven**, probably with kids, when records goes.
I'd still worry about **money in between**, while the wedding and house come first.
do: Keep the job and move to the **field side** in a few years.
Help my fiancé build a **family electrical business** with an apprentice.
feel: Anxious but **able to breathe**, with the wedding mattering more day to day.
S4.quote: AI tools would feel different if the business was ours and not head office forcing it on me. I'd still check everything by hand, though.
fieldNote: With ten years, her focus shifts to the **wedding and a house**.
She'd only touch AI in a **family business**, not for head office.
She notices the **bookkeeping** she'd do is also thinking work.

steps.text: Hold the August wedding at the church as planned
Help Tomas (her fiancé) take on an apprentice electrician
Ask Phil (her manager) about field-side jobs in three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to do anything except hope Tomas's work holds up. What would help is employers keeping people on and training them into hands-on jobs, not just letting them go. And apprenticeships for adults, not only for teenagers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith, and that matters to me. Whatever happens with AI, I'd still have my church and my family. That's not nothing when the job goes.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens with AI, I'd still have my church and my family. That's not nothing when the job goes.
portrait: Uma is a **27-year-old records team lead** at the regional water company, managing four people.
She's engaged to Tomas, an **electrician**, and their church wedding is next August.
She **distrusts AI** for safety reasons and has never used it.
She's **alarmed** in most scenarios, expecting her office job to go and leaning on family.
Her **faith and family** steady her, and she'd seek them before government help.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to act and only Tomas's job to rely on.
whatWouldHelp: Employers **retraining staff** into hands-on jobs instead of letting them go.
